newsitem.title: USA: Peru political crisis hurts credit ratings-Wall St.
newsitem.headline: Peru political crisis hurts credit ratings-Wall St.

text.p: The political crisis in Peru has constrained the country's credit rating and could even unravel the economic recovery, U.S. analysts said Thursday.

Wall Street investors would watch to how President Alberto Fujimori would react to his rapidly declining popularity, a series of cabinet resignations and allegations of corruption and rights abuses by the government and security forces.

U.S. analysts expected Fujimori to stick by his economic agenda, which yielded 7.2 percent GDP growth over the first five months of 1997, but that Peruvians should not expect any rapid improvement in the country's credit rating.

"The main constraint on the credit rating appears to be coming from the political side and what can be derivied from th political side onto economic performance," said Mauro Leos, senior analyst at Moody's Investor Service.
On a visit to New York last week, Peru's Finance Minister Jorge Camet forecast that Moody's would raise its B2 foreign currency debt rating by year end.
Standard & Poor's did not rate the country.
But Leos told Reuters the rating reflected events such as those seen at present.
"The improvement we have seen on the economic side is not sufficient to grant reconsideration, given the political problems," he said.

On Wednesday, Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela, one of the most respected figures in the cabinet, resigned reportedly to disassociate himself from a series of scandals, including claims of phone-tapping by the secret services and the removal of Peruvian citizenship for the Israeli-born owner of a local television channel critical of the military.

The government has held fiscal spending and monetary growth in check, but concerns remained about how the political turmoil would affect expectations, investment decisions and, in the end, on capital flows, Leos said. Wall Street investors may be prepared to wait and see what happens.

Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market analysis at Boston- based mutual fund company Scudder, Stevens Clark, said the political crisis was not likely to lead to any significant changes in economic policy.

"If we see more instability, where we see that policies cannot be executed, that would be a problem," Luis said. "As long as policies don't change, the effect on prices will be short lived. If people perceive policies cannot be continued, then obviously the price effects will be longer lasting."
Peru PDIs PEPDI=RR dropped 3/4 to 64-3/4, while the country's FLIRBS lost 7/8 to 59-1/2, in line with losses across the Brady bond market.

Siobhan Manning, economist at Santander Investments, said the markets would wait for Fujimori's speech to the nation on July 28, but added that the president was unlikely to compromise on the economy's fundamentals.

"The economic situation is very positive and I think some of the political instability is somewhat discounted," Manning said. "If things deteriorate to the point where Fujimori starts compromising economic policies for his own political ambitions, that's when you have to worry."
